generator.params.needle_years.why: A shoot keeps its foliage as long as its needles or scale leaves live.

generator.params.cone_years.why: A cone is drawn from its first season on the tree until it falls: the seasons it takes to ripen, then the years it hangs on once ripe.

generator.params.cone_pitch.why: Degrees down from its shoot: a negative pitch stands a cone up.

appearance.organs.cone.shape.aspect.why: A seed cone is drawn as wide across, closed, as it is stated, for its stated length.

appearance.organs.*.shape.bundle.why: A pine's needles in their bundles.

appearance.organs.*.shape.needle.why: A spray card draws its needles a share of its length, and a usual spray is about a fifth longer than the shortest shoot's (spray_base), measured over the conifers' cards at 60 years: so the usual needle is the stated one, up to the 0.4 a card holds.

appearance.organs.*.shape.ranks.why: Needles out all round the shoot, or in two flat ranks.

generator.params.wood_density.why: Green wood's density, its dry wood and the water it holds, which a limb's weight bends (bend@1).

generator.params.wood_modulus.why: Green wood's stiffness, which holds a limb up against its weight (bend@1).

generator.params.pipe_rings.why: No yearly rings on living foliage: a conifer's trunk is the pipe model's, its living foliage's pipes plus the disused pipes of the limbs it has shed (Shinozaki et al. 1964). Measured open-grown Douglas-fir (USDA Urban Tree Database, Longview, WA) are 58 cm through at 30 years and 95 cm at 60; the pipe model alone draws 56 and 93 cm, and every yearly ring rate added on top overgrew them (2.5e-5, fitted to McArdle's stands, drew 137 cm at 60 years; the old per-species 3e-5, 147 cm). The rates each species set by hand, 1.2e-6 to 3e-5, are gone.

generator.params.pipe_cambium.why: The stem's cambium lays a ring every year on the trunk it has, fed by the foliage above it: 3e-5 m² of ring a year for each m² of foliage times the share of the open sky's light it catches, whether or not the crown still grows. While the crown grows, the pipe model's trunk outgrows one year's ring, so young trees keep the pipe model's girth (open-grown Douglas-fir 96 cm at 60 years, as before; UTD 95); once an old crown stops growing the rings add up, and a 480-year Douglas-fir grown in a stand is 118 cm through (Ishii and McDowell 2002: 87 to 154 cm, mean 117, at 450 years), where the pipe model alone stopped at 74. Fed by light, a crown packed with shaded foliage (a Rocky Mountain juniper's, at a tenth of the sky's light) feeds little. Limbs keep the pipe model's girth.

traits.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Gymnosperms (DELTA, 2008 onwards, version of 5 August 2019), the conifer families: Araucariaceae, Cephalotaxaceae, Cupressaceae, Podocarpaceae, Sciadopityaceae and Taxaceae evergreen; Pinaceae mostly evergreen, the larches and golden larch deciduous; Taxodiaceae evergreen but for swamp cypress and dawn redwood, which shed their leafy shoots. Deciduous is the rare state.

generator.program.note: The conifers' own program (growth plan G2.3a), renamed from `conifer` and homed here: a leader laying down whorls of branches each year, with sprays of foliage and cones.

rules.note: Spec rework E6d: the pinidae program's foliage life, cones and needle bundles and ranks from each taxon's stated characters. Conifer sag (M6): green wood's density and stiffness from the Wood Handbook values the species state.

rules.generator.params.pipe_rings.note: McPherson, van Doorn and Peper (2016), Urban tree database (USDA Forest Service RDS-2016-0005), Pacific Northwest region (Longview, WA), 39 open-grown Douglas-fir 1 to 76 years old: dbh = -1.19688 + 2.36185 age - 0.01267 age² (adjusted r² 0.985), 58 cm at 30 years and 95 at 60; at 72 to 76 years, 88 to 118 cm. Shinozaki, Yoda, Hozumi and Kira (1964), A quantitative analysis of plant form: the pipe model theory: a stem carries a pipe for every unit of foliage above it, and keeps the disused pipes of branches that have died.

rules.generator.params.pipe_cambium.note: Ishii and McDowell (2002), Forest Ecology and Management 169: 257-270, Table 1: six 450-year Douglas-firs at Wind River, 87 to 154 cm dbh (mean 117), five 40-year trees 30 to 50 cm. Sillett et al. (2010), Forest Ecology and Management 259: 976-994: wood production of the whole tree keeps rising through old age in tall trees, while ring width at the base slows. Shaw et al. (2004), Ecosystems 7: 427: Wind River old growth, basal area 82.9 m2/ha. The rate is fitted to Ishii's mean with the open-grown references (USDA Urban Tree Database, Longview, WA) held.
